title: Probing the Potential Profile of Twisted Bilayer Graphene via Fabry-Pérot Interference
authors: Curtis McDowell, Alina Mreńca-Kolasińska, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming-Hao Liu, Thiti Taychatanapat
abstract: We use Fabry-Pérot interference to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. We trace anomalous resistance oscillations in the nominally unipolar regime to a hidden cavity formed by unintentional local doping in our device. By analyzing zero-field interference patterns, we determine the location and size of this inhomogeneity. Magnetotransport measurements support the model, distinguishing local cavity modes from global resonances through their different magnetic dependence. Simulations using our extracted profile reproduce the experimental features. Our results highlight interference spectroscopy as a simple, non-invasive probe for identifying local defects and internal potential barriers in ballistic devices.
summary: This work uses Fabry-Pérot interference measurements on twisted bilayer graphene to map out hidden potential barriers caused by unintentional local doping. By analyzing the characteristic resistance oscillations and their magnetic field dependence, the authors successfully model the precise spatial distribution of these charge inhomogeneities. This establishes interference spectroscopy as a powerful, non-destructive tool for characterizing internal defects in nanoscale quantum devices.
main_problem: The study aims to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) by identifying unintentional local doping that forms multiple electronic cavities.
main_result: The anomalous resistance oscillations are successfully attributed to localized, unintended doping creating distinct Fabry-Pérot cavities within the device structure. This method proves interference spectroscopy is a simple, non-invasive probe for mapping internal potential barriers.
method: Fabry-Pérot (FP) interference measurements using 2-probe resistance mapping ($R$ vs $V_{BG}, V_{TG}$) at zero magnetic field, supplemented by magnetotransport analysis and quantum transport simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is large-angle tBLG encapsulated in hBN. The model incorporates a local doping profile $n_i(x)$ derived from electrostatic analysis to simulate the resulting potential barriers and cavity structures.
key_observables: Anomalous resistance oscillations, secondary vertical/diagonal resistance peaks, and the magnetic field dependence of interference fringe spacing.
important_parameters: Low temperature ($T=2.4 	ext{ K}$), ballistic transport regime ($	ext{MFP} \sim 2 \mu	ext{m}$), and doping-induced cavity lengths (e.g., $L \approx 150$ nm, $L \approx 650$ nm).
main_assumptions: The observed oscillations are due to localized, unintentional doping forming potential barriers; the extracted profile is treated as a highly constrained model.
figures_summary: Figures show resistance maps ($R$ vs gates) revealing interference fringes (vertical/diagonal), and simulations map the derived potential profile $n_i(x)$ corresponding to these observed cavity structures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses transport measurements across different gate configurations (unipolar, bipolar) to observe characteristic Fabry-Pérot interference patterns. These patterns are then modeled by extracting a spatially varying doping profile $n_i(x)$, which is validated against both zero-field and magnetic field magnetotransport data.
why_interesting: The technique of using quantum interference spectroscopy to map static, unintentional charge inhomogeneities in 2D materials is highly valuable for understanding device physics beyond simple band structure calculations.

FIG. 3. (a, b) Experimental and simulated maps of the numerical derivative dR/dVTG versus B in the bipolar regime (VBG = 20 V). The interference fringes disperse and vanish for |B| > 0.2 T due to the cyclotron cutoff. (c, d) Experimental and simulated maps of dR/dVBG versus B at VTG = −8 V. The quasi-periodic fluctuations persist with weak dispersion to high fields, supporting confinement in a small, electronic cavity. (e, f) Calculated oscillation amplitude for (e) long (L = 650 nm) and (f) short (L = 150 nm) cavities. The model shows that the long-cavity mode is suppressed at low fields (B ≈0.2 T), while the short-cavity mode survives well beyond the measurement range.

FIG. 4. (a) Experimental map of the numerical derivative dR/dVTG at B = 0.1 T. Diagonal oscillations from the long central cavity extend into the unipolar regime (VBG < 0 V), where they coexist with sharp vertical fringes. A switching event is observed at VBG ≈12 V. (b) Simulated map of dR/dVTG at B = 0.1 T. The model qualitatively reproduces the key signature of the three-cavity series: the superposition of dispersive diagonal modes and vertical fringes in the unipolar region.
